title: Tab-and-slot journal closure
subtitle: Cutting an interlocking tab and slot in a soft journal cover
excerpt: A tab-and-slot closure cuts directly into the journal's soft cover to create a self-fastening flap. No hardware required: the tab tucks through the slot and friction holds it shut.
sourceNotes: Traditional soft-cover closure found in commercial stationery and hand-bound notebooks. No single pre-1928 text covers the cut-in-cover tab closure specifically; this entry synthesises the general technique from current soft-cover bookbinding practice.

glossaryTerms.definition: An extension of the back cover beyond the foredge of the text block, folded over the front of the book to form a closure.

content.text: A tab-and-slot closure works in a soft-cover journal where the back cover extends 40 to 60 mm past the foredge as a
. A tab is cut from the flap end and a matching slot is cut into the front cover. The tab tucks through the slot and holds the journal closed. The whole closure takes about five minutes to cut.

attrs.heading: Cutting tools safety
attrs.body: Sharp blades are safer than blunt blades. Cut on a self-healing cutting mat. Keep the non-cutting hand behind the line of cut.

items.name: A soft-cover journal with a foredge flap
items.notes: The back cover must already extend 40-60 mm past the foredge. If making the journal from scratch, add this extension when cutting the cover.

items.name: Craft knife + No. 11 blades
items.notes: Change the blade before cutting: a sharp blade is critical for a clean tab edge.

items.name: Self-healing cutting mat, A4
items.notes: Always under the cover when cutting.

items.name: Bone folder
items.notes: For scoring the flap fold-line cleanly.

content.text: Mark the tab on the foredge flap

Open the flap flat. Mark a tab centred on the flap end: 25 mm wide and 20 mm tall. The tab should be centred left-to-right across the flap. Cut the two vertical sides of the tab with the craft knife against the metal ruler, then cut the top horizontal line. Remove the small rectangles of waste on each side of the tab. The tab now stands proud of the flap end.
Cut the slot in the front cover

Close the journal and fold the flap over the front cover. Press the tab gently against the front cover to mark its position. Open the cover and cut a slot 26 mm wide and 4 mm tall at the marked position, centred horizontally to align with the tab. Cut cleanly with a single pass of the craft knife: the slot needs clean edges, not frayed paper. The slot should be 1 mm wider than the tab so it slides in and out without tearing.

Close the journal, fold the flap over, and tuck the tab through the slot. It should slide in with light thumb pressure and hold without springing out. If the tab is too wide to enter, widen the slot in 1 mm increments rather than narrowing the tab: trimming the tab weakens it. If the tab is so loose it drops out immediately, the slot is too tall. There is no clean fix for a slot that is too tall; cut a new slot 4 mm lower on the cover and mask the first slot from inside with a strip of matching paper glued over it.

items.symptom: The tab tears when pushed through the slot
items.cause: The tab is the same width as the slot, with no clearance, so it buckles under pressure.
items.fix: Widen the slot by 1 mm on each side with a fresh blade. Test again before widening further.

items.symptom: The tab drops out of the slot immediately
items.cause: The slot is too tall relative to the tab thickness, so there is insufficient friction.
items.fix: Thick cover stock rarely has this problem. For thin covers, cut a small strip from a matching scrap and glue it inside over the slot base. This reduces the slot height by 2 mm.

items.symptom: The slot is positioned too far from the foredge
items.cause: The flap was measured while under slight tension, pulling it shorter than its relaxed length.
items.fix: Mark the slot position with the journal fully closed and the flap folded flat under its own weight, not held flat by hand.
